blockMcqs.question: Which trio captures the OS's core jobs?
options: Compile, link, and load programs
Schedule CPU, page memory, guard hardware
Encrypt disk, route packets, render UI
Index files, cache pages, log events
blockMcqs.explanation: Every OS feature reduces to scheduling, virtual memory, or the privilege boundary.

blockMcqs.question: What do two threads in one process share that two processes don't?
options: Their program counters
Their register sets
The same address space
Their stacks
blockMcqs.explanation: Each thread keeps its own PC, registers, and stack; only the address space is shared.

blockMcqs.question: Which way do the stack and heap grow?
options: Both grow upward
Stack down, heap up, toward each other
Stack up, heap down
Both grow downward
blockMcqs.explanation: They expand into the free gap between them, which is why deep recursion collides.

blockMcqs.question: Why is a context switch's real cost more than the 1-5 µs save/restore?
options: The scheduler must sort all threads
Cold caches and a flushed TLB slow later accesses
Page tables get rebuilt from scratch
The disk is read on every switch
blockMcqs.explanation: The new thread runs slowly until its working set repopulates the caches and TLB.

blockMcqs.question: How does an MLFQ favor interactive work without manual priorities?
options: It runs threads strictly in arrival order
It demotes CPU-bound threads and keeps blockers high
It gives every thread an equal fixed quantum
It raises priority the longer a thread runs
blockMcqs.explanation: Threads that block quickly stay near the top, so interactive ones get served first.

blockMcqs.question: What happens on a TLB miss?
options: The instruction is silently skipped
The page is immediately swapped to disk
The hardware walks the page table in RAM
The process receives a segfault
blockMcqs.explanation: Only if that walk finds the page absent does a page fault then occur.

blockMcqs.question: Why is a system call costlier than an ordinary function call?
options: It always reads from disk
It allocates a new thread
It crosses the user-to-kernel privilege boundary
It recompiles the calling code
blockMcqs.explanation: Trapping in and validating crosses protection rings, which a plain call never does.

blockMcqs.question: What is a zombie process?
options: A process stuck waiting on I/O
A finished process whose exit code isn't yet reaped
A process swapped fully to disk
A thread spinning on a lock
blockMcqs.explanation: Its memory is freed but a table slot lingers until the parent calls wait().

blockMcqs.question: For huge I/O-bound concurrency, what beats a thread per request?
options: An async event loop
One process per request
Thousands of OS threads
A cooperative-only scheduler
blockMcqs.explanation: It avoids per-thread stacks and the context-switch storm of mass threading.

blockMcqs.question: Why does Chrome run each tab in its own OS process?
options: Processes switch faster than threads
To share memory between tabs cheaply
Address-space isolation contains crashes and exploits
Processes use less memory than threads
blockMcqs.explanation: A separate address space means one tab can't read or corrupt another's memory.

blockMcqs.question: Why won't extra threads speed up CPU-bound work in CPython?
options: Threads can't access the heap there
The GIL blocks two threads running bytecode at once
Python forbids creating threads
Page faults serialize all threads
blockMcqs.explanation: Use processes for CPU-bound parallelism when a global interpreter lock exists.
